unit.title: The car and the circuit
unit.summary: What an F1 car is, why downforce and drag trade off, and how drivers use a corner.

lessons.title: Anatomy of an F1 car
lessons.objective: Locate the main parts: wings, floor, halo, power unit, tyres.

payload.prompt: Where is the monocoque on this car?

diagram.alt: Top-down view of a Formula 1 car showing the chassis, wings and cockpit.

explanation.correct: Right. The monocoque is the carbon-fibre survival cell where the driver sits. It is the strongest part of the car and everything else bolts to it.
explanation.incorrect: The monocoque is the chassis around the driver. It is the strongest part, built from carbon fibre. The wings and engine bolt to it.
explanation.sayThisLine: The monocoque is the core of the car.

payload.prompt: What is the titanium bar above the cockpit?

diagram.alt: Side view of a Formula 1 car showing the cockpit, halo, engine and wings.

explanation.correct: Right. The halo is a titanium safety bar that protects the driver's head in a crash. It has saved drivers' lives many times since it was introduced in 2018.
explanation.incorrect: The halo is the titanium bar above the cockpit that protects the driver's head. It is bolted to the survival cell and has been protecting drivers since 2018.
explanation.sayThisLine: The halo has saved drivers many times.

payload.prompt: Where is the power unit (engine) on this car?

diagram.alt: Side view of a Formula 1 car showing the cockpit, halo, engine and wings.

explanation.correct: Right. The power unit is mounted behind the cockpit. It is not just 'the engine': F1 calls it a power unit because it combines a turbocharged V6 with electric motors and a battery.
explanation.incorrect: The power unit sits behind the cockpit. It is a turbocharged V6 plus electrical motors and a battery, which is why F1 does not just say 'engine'.
explanation.sayThisLine: It is a power unit, not just an engine.

payload.prompt: Match each car part to what it does.

pairs.definition: The carbon-fibre chassis where the driver sits; the strongest part of the car.
A titanium safety bar above the cockpit that protects the driver's head.
The turbocharged V6 engine plus electric motor and battery that drive the car.
Aerodynamic force from the wings and floor that pushes the car into the track.

distractorDefinitions: A device that reduces air resistance on the straights.
The rubber that grips the track.

explanation.summary: An F1 car is built around the monocoque, protected by the halo, powered by the power unit, and held down by downforce from its wings and floor.
explanation.sayThisLine: These parts make up the modern F1 car.

payload.prompt: What do the wings create?

pairs.definition: Creates downforce at the front to help steer and brake.
Creates downforce at the rear to increase grip and help the car accelerate.
The shaped underside that creates suction, pushing the car down as speeds increase.

distractorDefinitions: A system that reduces the car's weight.
A device that stores electrical energy.

explanation.summary: The front wing, rear wing and floor all work together to create downforce, which lets the car corner faster and brake harder.
explanation.sayThisLine: The wings and floor create downforce.

lessons.title: Downforce versus drag
lessons.objective: Explain why more wing means more grip but less top speed.

payload.prompt: What happens when a car runs more wing?

options.text: More downforce to grip, but more drag slows top speed.
options.explanation: Right. Bigger wings push the car down harder, so it corners faster. But the drag they create slows the straights.

options.text: More speed everywhere because more wing means more grip.
options.explanation: Grip is only part of it. More wing also brings drag, which costs speed on the straights.

options.text: No change, because downforce and drag cancel out.
options.explanation: They do not cancel. Both grow with more wing. It is a trade-off.

options.text: Faster in the pits but slower on track.
options.explanation: Pit speed is not related to wing angle. Wings affect on-track performance: grip and drag.

explanation.correct: Right. More wing = more downforce = faster through corners. But it also means more drag = slower on straights. Teams balance this with the track.
explanation.incorrect: More wing means more downforce, so the car grips and corners faster. But it also means more drag, so the car is slower on straights. It is always a trade-off.
explanation.sayThisLine: More wing, more grip, more drag. A trade-off.

payload.prompt: Which track usually gets the least wing of the season?

options.text: Monza, with long straights and few slow corners, so teams cut wing to save top speed.
options.explanation: Right. Monza is mostly full throttle, so teams trim the wings to cut drag.

options.text: Monaco, because tight corners need less grip.
options.explanation: Wrong. Monaco is slow and tight, so teams add wing for grip. It is the opposite of Monza.

options.text: Spa, because the weather is unpredictable.
options.explanation: Weather does not set the wing level. Spa has long straights and fast corners, so teams run a compromise rather than the least wing.

options.text: Every track uses the same wing because it is fixed by regulation.
options.explanation: No, teams adjust wings at every race. More wing for tight tracks, less wing for fast tracks.

explanation.correct: Right. Monza is largely flat out, so teams run as little wing as they can. It is the classic low-drag set-up.
explanation.incorrect: Low-drag setups are for tracks with long straights and high top-speed needs, like Monza. High-downforce setups are for tight tracks like Monaco.
explanation.sayThisLine: Monza runs the least wing of the season.

payload.prompt: Monaco is slow and twisty. Does it need a high-wing or low-wing set-up?

scene.alt: Tight corners at Monaco Grand Prix circuit.

explanation.correct: Right. Monaco's slow, tight corners reward maximum grip and downforce. There is hardly a straight long enough for drag to cost much.
explanation.incorrect: Monaco wants high downforce because the corners are so tight and slow. Top speed hardly matters there; grip and turning are what count.

payload.prompt: Does more drag cost more time on a straight or in a corner?

scene.alt: A car slowing down on a straight due to aerodynamic drag.

explanation.correct: Right. Drag grows quickly with speed, so it holds the car back most at high speed on the straights. In corners, grip from downforce matters far more.
explanation.incorrect: Drag costs the most time on straights where speed is highest. In corners the car is slower, so downforce matters more than drag.

payload.prompt: Roughly how much top speed does maximum wing cost versus a low-drag set-up?

explanation.correct: Close enough. It is a rough figure that varies by car and track, but a big wing typically costs a few tens of km/h on the straights. That is the trade-off teams juggle.
explanation.incorrect: As a rule of thumb, a big wing costs roughly 30 km/h of top speed. The exact number depends on the car and the track, but think 'tens of km/h', not a couple.
explanation.sayThisLine: More wing costs them a lot of top speed on the straights.

lessons.title: Monaco, Monza, Spa: circuit personalities
lessons.objective: Sort tracks by what they demand: downforce, top speed or traction.

payload.prompt: What makes a street circuit different from a permanent track?

options.text: Walls sit close to the track with little run-off, so one mistake can end the race.
options.explanation: Right. Street circuits are on closed public roads lined with barriers, so errors are expensive.

options.text: Street circuits are always slower than permanent tracks.
options.explanation: Not always: Baku has one of the longest straights on the calendar. The real difference is the walls.

options.text: Street circuits use different sized tyres than permanent tracks.
options.explanation: No, the same tyre compounds are used. The difference is the layout: walls and tight corners.

options.text: Street circuits have no qualifying, only practice and race.
options.explanation: Wrong. Street circuits have a full weekend with practice, qualifying and race, just on closed roads.

explanation.correct: Right. Street circuits are on public roads with walls and barriers instead of run-off, so a lock-up or spin can mean a crash. Monaco, Singapore and Baku are the classics.
explanation.incorrect: Street circuits are run on closed public roads with tight corners and walls right on the edge. Mistakes are punished hard.
explanation.sayThisLine: Monaco is a street circuit with no room for mistakes.

payload.prompt: What is a high-speed corner?

options.text: A corner that is taken flat or nearly flat, where downforce matters most, like Copse at Silverstone.
options.explanation: Right. High-speed corners are taken at race speed, so aerodynamic grip (downforce) is everything.

options.text: A corner where overtaking usually happens.
options.explanation: Overtaking tends to happen after slow corners and under braking. A high-speed corner is defined by speed, not by passing.

options.text: Any corner where the cars brake late.
options.explanation: Late braking is a separate idea. A high-speed corner is one where little or no braking is needed because the speed is carried.

options.text: A corner that changes direction twice, like a chicane.
options.explanation: That describes the shape, not the speed. Chicanes are usually slow, so they are not high-speed corners.

explanation.correct: Right. High-speed corners like Copse at Silverstone are taken flat or nearly flat. Downforce does the work.
explanation.incorrect: A high-speed corner is one where you do not brake; you carry speed through by relying on aerodynamic grip (downforce).
explanation.sayThisLine: This corner is so fast, taken flat out.

payload.prompt: A hairpin is a 180-degree corner at the end of a straight. Do drivers brake hard for it?

scene.alt: A tight 180-degree hairpin turn at the end of a long straight.

explanation.correct: Right. Hairpins are slow corners after long straights, so drivers brake hard, turn tight, and accelerate out. They are often overtaking spots.
explanation.incorrect: Hairpins are slow, tight 180s, so yes, drivers brake hard to slow down from race speed to corner speed.

payload.prompt: Do drivers use kerbs (the painted ramps at corner edges) to make a better line?

scene.alt: A bright painted kerb at the edge of a corner showing the racing line.

explanation.correct: Right. Drivers use kerbs to flatten the line and carry speed. But too much kerb can unsettle the car and cost time.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, drivers use kerbs to widen their arc and keep speed up. But they have to be careful: too much kerb can bounce or break the suspension.

payload.prompt: Match each track type to its main challenge.

pairs.definition: Tight, bumpy, walls close; one mistake and you crash into a barrier.
Flowing corners taken near race speed; downforce and aerodynamic grip are critical.
A slow, tight 180-degree corner, usually at the end of a straight; a common overtaking spot.

distractorDefinitions: A track with a lot of run-off for mistakes.
A track where the straights are longer than the corners.

explanation.summary: Different circuits demand different skills: street circuits need precision, high-speed tracks need confidence, and hairpins need late braking.
explanation.sayThisLine: Each circuit has its own personality.

lessons.title: The racing line
lessons.objective: Show that the fastest path is the widest arc, not the shortest.

payload.prompt: Why is the racing line wider than the shortest path through a corner?

options.text: A wide entry and exit let you carry more speed than cutting tight to the apex.
options.explanation: Right. The racing line is wide in, clip the apex, wide out. This keeps speed up.

options.text: A wider line reduces the risk of crashing into the wall.
options.explanation: Safety is not the reason. The racing line is faster because it is the smoothest path.

options.text: To leave more room for rivals on the inside.
options.explanation: Room for rivals is a side effect at best. The line is chosen because it lets the car carry the most speed.

options.text: Tighter lines are only used during practice; in the race it is different.
options.explanation: No, the racing line is the same in practice and race. It is the fastest path every time.

explanation.correct: Right. The racing line sacrifices the shortest distance for the smoothest arc. Wide in, apex, wide out means you are turning less sharply and can keep higher speed.
explanation.incorrect: The racing line is not the shortest path through a corner; it is the fastest. A wider, smoother arc means less steering, so the car carries more speed.
explanation.sayThisLine: The racing line is wide in, clip the apex, wide out.

payload.prompt: Complete the sentence about the apex.
payload.template: The apex is the point on the {{side}} of a corner where the car passes {{closest}} to the kerb.

explanation.correct: Right. The apex is the point on the inside of the corner where the car gets closest to the kerb. Clipping it smoothly is the key to carrying speed.
explanation.incorrect: The apex sits on the inside of the corner, and the car passes closest to the kerb there. The exit is the outside edge, and braking comes before the turn.
explanation.sayThisLine: He clipped the apex and carried speed.

payload.prompt: In a braking-zone corner before a straight, is hitting a late apex better for exit speed?

scene.alt: A corner followed by a long straight, showing a late apex and early exit to the straight.

explanation.correct: Right. A late apex (hitting the corner deeper before turning) lets you exit wider and straighter, so you can accelerate harder onto the next straight.
explanation.incorrect: Yes. A late apex means you turn later, which lets you exit wider and accelerate sooner onto the straight. It is slower mid-corner but faster overall.

lessons.title: Brake, turn, throttle
lessons.objective: Describe the three phases of a corner and where speed is won.

payload.prompt: What is the order of a braking-zone corner?

items.text: Brake hard on the straight to slow the car.
items.why: Braking zone: slowing down from race speed to corner speed.

items.text: Turn in at the right point to hit the apex on the racing line.
items.why: Entry: follow the racing line to the apex.

items.text: Ease off the brakes as you turn to avoid losing grip.
items.why: Trail braking: balancing braking and turning through the apex.

items.text: Accelerate hard out of the corner to gain speed on the exit.
items.why: Exit: power onto the straight for the next sector.

explanation.correct: Right. Brake hard, turn in, trail the brakes through the apex, then accelerate out. That is the cornering sequence.
explanation.incorrect: A corner is: brake on the straight, turn at the right point to hit the apex, trail brake (ease off while turning), then accelerate out hard.

payload.prompt: Why is the braking zone the main overtaking spot?

options.text: A follower can brake later than the car ahead and get alongside on the inside.
options.explanation: Right. Cars arrive at high speed, so a driver who is brave enough to brake later can pull level before the corner.

options.text: Overtaking is easier on the brakes because both cars are slower.
options.explanation: Cars are not slow at the start of the braking zone; they arrive at top speed. The chance comes from who brakes later, not from being slow.

options.text: The leader always brakes later, so the follower has no chance.
options.explanation: The leader does not always get to decide. A follower with a good run can brake later still, and the leader has to choose between defending and taking a safe line.

options.text: Overtaking is banned on straights, so it must happen under braking.
options.explanation: No, overtaking is allowed on straights. But the braking zone is the main spot because late braking works.

explanation.correct: Right. Braking is where speed differences show up. A follower who brakes later can get alongside on the inside, and the car ahead has to decide whether to defend or give up the place.
explanation.incorrect: The braking zone is the main overtaking spot because a driver behind can brake later than the leader and pull alongside on the inside before the corner.
explanation.sayThisLine: The braking zone is where you pass.

payload.prompt: What is trail braking?

options.text: Carrying some brake pressure into the corner to help the car rotate.
options.explanation: Right. Trail braking is easing the brake gradually as you turn, not dumping the brakes all at once.

options.text: Braking in a straight line after the corner to slow for the next one.
options.explanation: That is ordinary braking on the straight. Trail braking happens as the car turns in, carrying brake into the corner.

options.text: Leaving the brake pedal alone until the car is fully turned.
options.explanation: That is the opposite. Trail braking keeps some brake pressure on while the car is turning in, then eases it off gradually.

options.text: Braking only on the exit to set up the next corner.
options.explanation: That is preparation for the next corner. Trail braking happens in the current corner.

explanation.correct: Right. Trail braking is carrying brake pressure into the corner to help the car turn. It keeps the weight on the front tyres and improves grip mid-corner.
explanation.incorrect: Trail braking means easing the brake gradually as you turn, not lifting off all at once. It is a smooth technique that keeps turning grip.
explanation.sayThisLine: He is trail braking deep into the corner.

payload.prompt: Complete the sentence about traction.
payload.template: Traction is the grip of the {{tyres}} tyres that lets a car put power down on the {{where}} without wheelspin.

explanation.correct: Right. Traction is rear-tyre grip on the way out of a corner. With good traction a car can get on the power early; with poor traction the wheels spin and time is lost.
explanation.incorrect: Traction is about acceleration grip, mostly through the rear tyres on the corner exit. Steering grip and braking grip are different things.
explanation.sayThisLine: He has great traction on the exit.

lessons.title: Understeer and oversteer
lessons.objective: Identify each from a description and say what drivers do about it.

payload.prompt: In understeer, which end of the car runs out of grip? Tap it.

diagram.alt: Top-down view of a Formula 1 car, front wing at the top, with the front tyres, cockpit and rear tyres marked.

explanation.correct: Right. Understeer is when the front tyres run out of grip, so the car will not turn as much as the driver asks and pushes wide.
explanation.incorrect: Understeer is a front-tyre problem: the front does not grip enough to turn, so the car pushes wide. A rear that steps out is oversteer, the opposite.

payload.prompt: In oversteer, which end of the car loses grip and slides? Tap it.

diagram.alt: Top-down view of a Formula 1 car, front wing at the top, with the front tyres, cockpit and rear tyres marked.

explanation.correct: Right. Oversteer is when the rear tyres lose grip and step out, so the car turns more than the driver asked and risks a spin.
explanation.incorrect: Oversteer is a rear-tyre problem: the rear runs out of grip and slides, so the car rotates too much. A front that pushes wide is understeer, the opposite.

payload.prompt: A driver has understeer (the car will not turn in). Which front-wing change helps?

scene.alt: A car pushing wide through a corner due to understeer.

explanation.correct: Right. Understeer means the front has no grip. Adding wing (downforce) gives the front more grip to turn.
explanation.incorrect: To fix understeer, add downforce (wing) at the front. More wing means more grip, which helps the car turn in.

payload.prompt: A driver has oversteer (rear sliding). Does the team soften or stiffen the rear suspension?

scene.alt: A car with the rear sliding out through a corner.

explanation.correct: Right. Oversteer means the rear is sliding. Softening the suspension lets the rear grip the track better, so the rear stops sliding out.
explanation.incorrect: To fix oversteer, soften the rear suspension. A softer rear lets the rear tyre keep better contact with the track.

payload.prompt: In a high-speed corner (flat out), is traction (rear grip on exit) more important than top speed on the straight?

scene.alt: A car exiting a high-speed corner onto a straight.

explanation.correct: Right. In a high-speed corner, traction (the ability to put power down) is more important than raw top speed. Good traction lets you exit faster.
explanation.incorrect: Yes. Traction on the exit gives you a better run onto the next straight. A car with no traction spins and loses more than a car with low top speed.

payload.prompt: A driver says: 'The front is gone, I cannot turn it.' What is this?

options.text: Understeer: the front tyres have no grip and the car will not turn in.
options.explanation: Right. 'Cannot turn it' is the classic understeer complaint. The front is washing out.

options.text: Oversteer: the rear is sliding out.
options.explanation: Oversteer is when the rear slides. The front going is understeer.

options.text: A broken steering rack.
options.explanation: A mechanical issue would be 'steering is broken'. This is a handling complaint, so it is understeer or oversteer.

options.text: Too much speed for the corner.
options.explanation: Speed affects handling, but 'the front is gone' is the language for understeer, not just going too fast.

explanation.correct: Right. 'The front is gone' and 'I cannot turn it' are understeer complaints. The front tyres are not gripping.
explanation.incorrect: Understeer is when the driver cannot turn in. The front washes out and the car ploughs straight. 'The front is gone' is the radio way to say it.

payload.prompt: A driver says: 'The rear is loose.' What is this?

options.text: Oversteer: the rear tyres are sliding and the car is turning too much.
options.explanation: Right. 'The rear is loose' means the rear is sliding, which is oversteer.

options.text: Understeer: the front is not gripping.
options.explanation: Understeer is a front problem. 'The rear is loose' is oversteer.

options.text: A mechanical problem with the suspension.
options.explanation: A loose rear can be caused by setup, but the driver is describing a handling issue, not a mechanical fault.

options.text: Good balance and the car is responding well.
options.explanation: Loose is not good. It means the rear is sliding, which is oversteer and hurts lap time.

explanation.correct: Right. 'The rear is loose' means oversteer. The rear is sliding, so the car is turning more than asked.
explanation.incorrect: Oversteer is when the rear is loose and sliding. The car turns too much and risks a spin. That is what the driver is reporting.
explanation.sayThisLine: The rear is loose, he is struggling with oversteer.

lessons.title: Reading the timing screen
lessons.objective: Read sectors, gaps, intervals and the purple, green and yellow times.

payload.prompt: What is a sector on the timing screen?

options.text: One third of the lap, timed separately; purple/green/yellow show who is quickest in each sector.
options.explanation: Right. A lap is split into three sectors. Timing is displayed per sector so you can see where speed is gained or lost.

options.text: The pit lane and the section before it.
options.explanation: No. Sectors are on-track only, three per lap.

options.text: A group of corners that take the same amount of time.
options.explanation: Not intentionally. A sector is one third of the lap distance.

options.text: The area where the marshal flags are posted.
options.explanation: That is a marshalling post. Sectors are timing sections of the track.

explanation.correct: Right. Sectors split the lap into three equal parts (distance-wise). The timing display shows each sector separately so you can see who is quick where.
explanation.incorrect: A lap is split into three sectors. Each sector is timed separately. Purple means fastest, green means fast, yellow means less fast.
explanation.sayThisLine: He set a purple sector time.

payload.prompt: What is the difference between gap and interval?

options.text: Gap is the time to the leader; interval is the time to the car ahead.
options.explanation: Right. Gap tells you how far behind the leader you are. Interval tells you the gap to the car directly ahead.

options.text: Gap is on the straights; interval is in the corners.
options.explanation: No. Both are measured over a full lap. Where you measure does not change the definition.

options.text: They mean the same thing; the terms are interchangeable.
options.explanation: No. Gap is to the leader; interval is to the car ahead (even if they are in 15th).

options.text: Gap is the distance in metres; interval is in seconds.
options.explanation: Both are in seconds (or tenths). The difference is who you are measuring to.

explanation.correct: Right. The gap is the time between you and the leader. The interval is the time between you and the car directly ahead.
explanation.incorrect: Gap = time to the leader. Interval = time to the car ahead (position + 1). You check the gap to see if you can catch the leader; you check the interval for your immediate fight.
explanation.sayThisLine: He is five seconds behind the leader.

payload.prompt: What does a purple sector mean?

options.text: The fastest sector time overall in the race or session.
options.explanation: Right. Purple is the benchmark: it is the fastest anyone has been in that sector.

options.text: The driver is in the lead of the race.
options.explanation: No. Purple is about pace in a sector, not overall position.

options.text: The tyres are in a good temperature range.
options.explanation: Tyre temperature is not shown on sector times. Purple is just the fastest pace.

options.text: The driver is on a qualifying lap in the race.
options.explanation: Purple can happen in any session. It is just the fastest sector time.

explanation.correct: Right. Purple is the fastest. If someone sets a purple sector, they have just beaten the fastest time anyone has set in that sector.
explanation.incorrect: Purple means fastest in that sector, anywhere in the session. If you see purple, that driver is going very quick in that part of the track.
explanation.sayThisLine: Purple sector, he is really quick through there.

payload.prompt: Fill in the blank: 'He is trailing the leader by _____, but his interval to the car ahead is only two seconds.'
payload.template: He is trailing the leader by {{gap-time}}, but his interval to the car ahead is only two seconds.

explanation.correct: Right. If the gap to the leader is 15 seconds and the interval to the car ahead is 2 seconds, then there is a 13-second gap between P2 and P3.
explanation.incorrect: The gap is time to the leader. The interval is time to the car ahead. If interval is 2s and the gap is 15s, the car is in 3rd, 13 seconds behind 2nd.

payload.prompt: Fill in the blank: 'The leader is 20 seconds ahead and the _____ to the second-place car is 3 seconds.'
payload.template: The leader is 20 seconds ahead and the {{term}} to the second-place car is 3 seconds.

explanation.correct: Right. The interval is the time to the car directly ahead. The leader is 20s ahead overall (gap), and P2 is 3s ahead (interval).
explanation.incorrect: The interval is the time to the car ahead. Since the leader is 20s clear, the interval to P2 is what someone in 3rd sees.

payload.prompt: If three purple sectors are 38s, 42s and 40s, what would be the best possible lap time?

explanation.correct: Right. Three purples of 38 + 42 + 40 = 120 seconds for the lap. That is the theoretical best lap if all three purple sectors happened in the same lap.
explanation.incorrect: Add them up: 38 + 42 + 40 = 120 seconds. That would be a lap time of 2 minutes. Each sector is timed from one point to the next, so the lap is the sum of all three.
explanation.sayThisLine: The lap time is the sum of the three sector times.

lessons.title: DRS: what it was and why it went
lessons.objective: Explain the old overtaking flap and why it was replaced.

payload.prompt: What did DRS do?

options.text: Opened a flap on the rear wing to cut drag and gain top speed when overtaking.
options.explanation: Right. DRS (Drag Reduction System) opened to allow a tow car within one second to use extra speed on the straight.

options.text: Added extra fuel for a power boost.
options.explanation: No. DRS was purely aerodynamic. It reduced drag by opening the wing.

options.text: Automatically braked a leading car so the follower could pass.
options.explanation: That would be illegal. DRS just cut the drag of the chasing car to help it overtake.

options.text: Replaced the tyres with slick compounds for wet weather.
options.explanation: DRS had nothing to do with tyres. It was a rear-wing flap that reduced drag.

explanation.correct: Right. DRS was a flap on the rear wing that opened to cut drag. A car within one second of the leader could activate it in certain zones.
explanation.incorrect: DRS (Drag Reduction System) was a movable flap on the rear wing. When open, it cut drag and let the overtaking car go faster on straights.
explanation.sayThisLine: DRS is gone. It is Overtake Mode now.

payload.prompt: Why was DRS introduced in 2011?

options.text: The 2009 rule changes created more downforce, so dirty air was choking overtaking. DRS was an aid.
options.explanation: Right. More wing = more downforce, but also more wake and dirty air behind the car. DRS helped the follower break through.

options.text: Engines were getting too slow, so DRS added power.
options.explanation: DRS did not add power. Engines were fine. It was a downforce problem.

options.text: Tyres were not lasting long enough.
options.explanation: DRS helped overtaking, not tyre life.

options.text: Pit stops were taking too long.
options.explanation: Pit stops improved through crew efficiency, not DRS.

explanation.correct: Right. The 2009 rule changes added a lot of downforce and created a dirty-air problem. Following cars lost grip and could not overtake. DRS was the band-aid.
explanation.incorrect: DRS was invented because following cars could not pass due to dirty air (turbulent wake). The wing created so much downforce that the follower was stuck.
explanation.sayThisLine: DRS was a crutch for overtaking.

payload.prompt: Why was DRS removed for 2026?

options.text: Active aero (Straight Mode) is a better answer: wings adjust all lap, and Overtake Mode is a boost for the whole car.
options.explanation: Right. DRS was a one-tool solution. Active aero is more dynamic and fair.

options.text: Overtaking was too easy and races were boring.
options.explanation: Actually, DRS made some races predictable. The new system is meant to improve racing.

options.text: The rear wing became too small and DRS did not fit.
options.explanation: Size is not the issue. The FIA wanted a better system for a new regulation era.

options.text: Engines became too powerful for DRS to help.
options.explanation: Power levels are controlled. DRS was removed for strategic reasons, not power.

explanation.correct: Right. DRS was a one-trick fix for dirty air. Active aero is better: wings adjust all lap for better balance, and Overtake Mode is a driver tool.
explanation.incorrect: DRS was removed because active aero (Straight Mode) is a better solution for the 2026 cars. It lets drivers choose when to open the wings, not just in DRS zones.
explanation.sayThisLine: DRS was a band-aid. Active aero is the real fix.

payload.prompt: Is DRS history now, or does it still matter in 2026?

scene.alt: A 2026 F1 car with active aero instead of DRS.

explanation.correct: Right. DRS is gone. It was retired at the end of 2025. 2026 uses active aero and Overtake Mode instead.
explanation.incorrect: DRS is retired as of 2026. It is history. The new cars use active aero (Straight Mode / Corner Mode) and Overtake Mode for overtaking.

payload.prompt: Did drivers have to be close to use DRS?

scene.alt: Two cars on a straight: one trailing within the DRS zone.

explanation.correct: Right. DRS could only be used within one second of the car ahead (in DRS zones). If you were trailing by more than one second, DRS was locked.
explanation.incorrect: Yes. DRS was only allowed if the car was within one second of the leader. It was a follower's tool, not a general speed boost.
